full_judgment:
3. Plaintiff instituted other Class Suit No.44 of 1995 for partition on declaring nullity of a deed against the appellant Md. Shamsul Haque and others. Plaint case in short is that on Md. Chulai was the original owner of 2.07 acres of land by purchase from one Sattar Mia by kabala dated 18th April, 1952. Said Md. Chulai died leaving 06 sons, wife Sakhina and another wife Rabeya who died during his life time. Three sons of Md. Chulai namely Md. Rawshan, Md. Asgor and Md. Sabdar through Chulai's predeceased wife rabeya sold out their entire 7 (seven) anal share of 90 decimals to one Min Uddin and Akbar by registered kabala dated 13th December, 1972. Said Alim Uddin and Akbar subsequently sold the said 90 decimals of land to the defendant Shamsul Haque in 1988. The remaining 1.17 acres of land remained in the possession of Chuli's other three sons Md. Jabbar, Md. Sattar Mia and Md. Abbas and wife Sakhina Khatun. Subsequently Md. Abbas died unmarried and his other two full brothers Md. Jabbar and Sattar Mia and mother Sakhina Khatun inherited his share. While Md. Jabbar, Md., Sattar Mia and their mother Sakhina Khatun were in possession of their 1.17 acres of land, they came to know in the middle part of 1994 that 06 decimals land out of their 1.17 acres were acquired by the government for the purpose of construction of a bypass road and that the defendant Shamsul Haque, by creating a false deed was trying to receive the compensation money Md. Jabbar, Md. Sattar and their mother then procured the certified copy of the deed and confirmed that Shamsul, Haque created the deed by false personation. 

 5. Defendant No.1 (defendant) Shamsul Haque contested that suit by filling written statement. His case is that the plaintiffs sold said 1.1.7 acres of land to him in the year 1974 at a consideration of taka 2000/-and delivered possession; that though a sale deed was executed on 25,08.1974, it could not have been registered for want of necessary permission of the government which was necessary during the relevant time for transferring 'Bihari refugess' land that after withdrawal of that restriction, the deed was registered in favour of the defendant and that the defendant has been possessing this 1.17 acres of land for more than 20 years by exercising his right little and interest therein. 

 7. Though the plaintiff's claim partition and entitlement of compensation money assessed by the Government in L.A. Case No. 69 of 1993-94 the only point requires to be considered is whether the defendant has acquired title b adverse possession in the suit land. It the defendant's plea of adverse possession is established, the plaintiffs cannot get a decree as prayed for. 

 9. There is no dispute that a person cannot claim title by adverse possession in the land in dispute on the basis of an agreement even if his possession exceeds over the statutory period. To constitute title by adverse possessions, the claimant must prove his hostile possession over statutory period to the knowledge of the real owner. The High Court Division, Therefore, has rightly observed, that to constitute adverse possession, One must be in possession for the statutory period openly, in assertion of his own title as owner and denying the title of the true owner, and such open hostile possession, under claim of ownership, must be to the knowledge of the true owner; mere possession without the necessary ingredients of adverse possessions however long continued, does not and cannot ripen into title by adverse possessions ". In talking the above views it has relied upon the case of Dalimunessa Bewa V. Md. Hashmat Ali. 61 DLR (AD) 8. 

 13. If the possession is actual, open, uninterrupted, notorious, exclusive and continuous over a statutory period, it confers an indefeasible title upon the possessor. The extent of the title acquired by adverse possession depends on the extent of the claim or right under which possession is obtained and kept, To constitute possession in the claim of the possessor must of be effectively realised in the facts, It is sufficient if the possession is overt without any attempt of concealment. That possession to the extent to which it is capable of demonstration must be hostile, notorious and exclusive to make it adverse and will only extend to the land in actual occupation of the wrong doer. All these elements of hostile possessions are present in this case and the defendant has been able to prove it by oral and documentary evidence, The trial Court has rightly held the extinguishment of plaintiff's title by adverse possession. 

 16. The High Court Division has totally overlooked the facts-proved by the defendant in support of his claim of hostile possession and on misconception of law it has affirmed the judgment of the court of appeal below. The case considered by the High Court Division squarely supports the case of the defendant. The High Court Division misconstrued the decision in failing to consider that in that case, it has been held that if there is a complete ouster by asserting hostile title the plaintiff's title is extinguished, inasmuch as, he has lost his title by the acts of the defendant who having been in possession denying the plaintiff's title openly.
